briefing.title: Rome, 753 BC – AD 391
paragraphs: Picture Rome as its people saw it: a city that owed every victory to the gods. Romans struck a deal with heaven, "I give, that you might give", offering sacrifices and exact prayers in return for protection, harvests and triumph. Aristocrats doubled as priests, augurs watched the birds, and six Vestals guarded a sacred flame.

Over eleven centuries, from legendary founders to Christian emperors, Rome welcomed foreign gods, turned its rulers into gods, and finally collided with a faith that rejected all others. Get the ritual wrong, Romans believed, and the whole state paid the price.

timelines.name: Turning Points
timelines.blurb: Four milestones from Rome's legendary founding to the last of the old festivals.

events.label: Romulus founds Rome
events.fact: According to tradition, the twins first consulted the gods by watching birds before building the new city.

events.label: Great Mother brought to Rome
events.fact: During Rome's second war against Carthage, the sacred prophecy books advised bringing in this goddess from Asia Minor.

events.label: Edict of Milan proclaims toleration
events.fact: Under Constantine, the emperor who converted to Christianity, the Edict of Milan proclaimed toleration.

events.label: Church council bans the Parentalia
events.fact: The February festival honouring family ancestors was so popular that Christians attended it until a church council forbade it.

timelines.name: Republic to Empire
timelines.blurb: Six moments from the wars with Carthage to Christianity's victory.

events.label: Consul throws sacred chickens overboard
events.fact: The chickens refused to eat before a sea battle; the consul joked they could drink instead, then lost the battle and his career.

events.label: Senate cracks down on the Bacchanalia
events.fact: Romans distrusted secrecy, so the wildly popular rites of the wine god Bacchus were placed under strict state control.

events.label: Julius Caesar chosen chief priest
events.fact: Becoming pontifex maximus was a sign of Caesar's rise; he later became the only Roman known to be treated as a god while alive.

events.label: Sailors at Naples hail Augustus
events.fact: They cried: "Because of you we are living, because of you we can travel the seas."

events.label: Great Fire of Rome
events.fact: The emperor of the day blamed the Christians, and persecution followed.

events.label: Christianity becomes official religion
events.fact: Under Theodosius, Christianity as defined at Nicaea became the official religion of the empire.

timelines.name: From Troy to the Last Flame
timelines.blurb: Eight events spanning legend, kings and emperors. Watch the late-empire dates closely.

events.label: Aeneas escapes burning Troy
events.fact: The Trojan prince, son of Venus, sailed to Italy carrying Troy's household gods and the Palladium, a holy statue.

events.label: Romulus kills Remus as walls rise
events.fact: The brothers quarrelled while their new city's walls were being built.

events.label: Numa keeps Janus's doors shut
events.fact: The doors of the Temple of Janus stood open in war and closed in peace; under the peaceful Numa they stayed shut.

events.label: Etruscan king founds Capitoline temple
events.fact: After Numa, an Etruscan king was credited with founding the great temple on the Capitoline Hill.

events.label: Edicts order churches destroyed
events.fact: New edicts commanded that churches and Christian books be destroyed; some Christians were imprisoned or executed.

events.label: Constantine dies, Christian and deified
events.fact: Though he had converted, Constantine was honoured at death both as a Christian and as a deified emperor.

events.label: Constantine's nephew revives old cults
events.fact: The new emperor tried to bring back the old cults but died in Persia two years later.

events.label: Theodosius puts out the Vestals' fire
events.fact: Theodosius ended state support for all other cults and extinguished Vesta's sacred flame.

matchSets.name: Gods with Jobs
matchSets.blurb: Rome's heaven was crowded with gods who each had a practical task. Match each god to their role.

pairs.name: Janus
pairs.match: Two-faced god of doorways; his temple doors stood open in wartime

pairs.name: Vesta
pairs.match: Goddess of the hearth whose sacred flame six priestesses tended

pairs.name: Quirinus
pairs.match: Patron of the citizens in peacetime, part of the Archaic Triad

matchSets.name: Priests and Rituals
matchSets.blurb: Roman religion ran on specialists and exact procedures. Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.name: Pontifex maximus
pairs.match: Chief priest, head of Rome's experts in religious law

pairs.name: Augurs
pairs.match: Read the will of the gods through the flight of birds

pairs.name: Haruspex
pairs.match: Inspected entrails, especially the liver, an Etruscan art

pairs.name: Mola salsa
pairs.match: Salted flour sprinkled on each animal before sacrifice

pairs.name: Do ut des
pairs.match: "I give, that you might give": the deal behind Roman religion

trueFalseDecks.name: Legends, Kings and Priests
trueFalseDecks.blurb: From Troy's refugees to Rome's sacred chickens.

cards.claim: Aeneas, the Trojan prince who sailed to Italy, was the son of the goddess Venus.
cards.why: Legend made Aeneas the son of Venus. Julius Caesar later claimed descent from her through him.

cards.claim: Romulus and Remus were said to be the sons of Jupiter.
cards.why: Their mother became pregnant by Mars, the god of war.

cards.claim: King Numa was said to take advice from Egeria, a nymph of springs and prophecy.
cards.why: Legend says Numa dealt directly with the gods, with Egeria as his divine companion.

cards.claim: Under Numa, the doors of the Temple of Janus stood open.
cards.why: The doors were open in wartime and closed in peace. Under the peaceful Numa they stayed shut.

cards.claim: When a magistrate forgot to mention "the Roman people" in a festival prayer, the whole festival had to start again.
cards.why: Prayers had to be exact, and a single slip could spoil a ritual.

cards.claim: The Capitoline Triad was made up of Jupiter, Juno and Ceres.
cards.why: It was Jupiter, his wife Juno and his daughter Minerva, goddess of wisdom.

cards.claim: The consul who threw the sacred chickens overboard in 249 BC went on to win the sea battle.
cards.why: He lost the battle, and his career with it.

cards.claim: A Vestal found to have broken her vow of chastity was buried alive.
cards.why: Vestals had extraordinary status, but their vow of chastity was strictly enforced.

trueFalseDecks.name: Foreign Gods, Emperors and Christians
trueFalseDecks.blurb: From the Great Mother to the end of the old cults.

cards.claim: In 206 BC Rome's sacred prophecy books advised bringing in the Great Mother from Asia Minor.
cards.why: She arrived during Rome's desperate second war against Carthage.

cards.claim: Mithras became a favourite god of sailors.
cards.why: Mithras was a favourite of soldiers, with shrines as far away as Britain.

cards.claim: Women were completely barred from the rites of the Good Goddess.
cards.why: It was men who were completely barred from the rites of the Good Goddess.

cards.claim: The Parentalia, a festival honouring family ancestors, was held each February.
cards.why: It lasted several days and stayed popular with Christians for centuries.

cards.claim: Julius Caesar claimed the goddess Juno as his ancestress.
cards.why: Caesar claimed descent from Venus, through her son Aeneas.

cards.claim: After an emperor's death, the Senate could vote him a god (divus).
cards.why: While he was alive, an emperor was honoured through his genius, the divine spirit in every person.

cards.claim: Constantine's nephew, who tried to revive the old cults, died in Egypt.
cards.why: He became emperor in 361 and died in Persia two years later.

cards.claim: In 380, under Theodosius, Christianity became the official religion of the empire.
cards.why: It was Christianity as defined at Nicaea. In 391 Theodosius ended state support for all other cults.

oddOneOut.why: Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus made up the Archaic Triad. Juno belonged to the later Capitoline Triad.
Juno of Veii, the Great Mother and Isis came to Rome from outside. Quirinus was one of Rome's own earliest gods.
Tradition credits Numa with the calendar, the Vestals and the Temple of Janus. The Capitoline temple was founded by a later Etruscan king.
Grovelling, excessive devotion and prying were condemned as superstition. Exact wording was essential to correct worship.
The other three were Vestal duties. Reading birds was the job of the augurs.
Three were measures against Christians. The Edict of Milan in 313 proclaimed toleration.
Three were ways of caring for the dead. The Bacchanalia were rites of the wine god Bacchus.

whoAmI.name: Founders of Legend
whoAmI.blurb: Figures from Rome's mythical beginnings, where history and legend blur.

people.name: Aeneas
clues: Romans believed the Vestals still guarded treasures I had carried.
In Italy I married a local king's daughter.
I brought the Palladium, a holy statue said to protect a city, across the sea.
I escaped from Troy when the Greeks destroyed it.

people.name: Romulus
clues: I was credited with Rome's first victory parade.
I built Rome's first temple to Jupiter.
I never died a normal death: I was carried off and made a god.
While the walls were rising, I killed my twin brother.

people.name: Numa
clues: I created flamens, priests each devoted to a single god.
I was a Sabine, from a hill people north-east of Rome.
A nymph of springs and prophecy was my divine companion.
As Rome's peaceful second king, I kept the doors of Janus shut.

whoAmI.name: Rulers and the Gods
whoAmI.blurb: Four leaders who reshaped Roman religion.

people.name: Julius Caesar
clues: In 63 BC I was chosen chief priest.
A comet seen during games after my death was taken as proof I had joined the gods.
I am the only Roman known to have been treated as a god while still alive.
A conquering general, I became dictator, claimed Venus as my ancestress and was murdered.
reviewFlags: "Julius Caesar" appears fewer than 2 times in the chapter

people.name: Augustus
clues: Shortly before my death in AD 14, sailors at Naples hailed me.
I boosted the Vestals' funding and gave them seats of honour at the games.
The doors of the Temple of Janus, open for centuries, closed in my reign.
Heir to a murdered dictator, I became Rome's first emperor.

people.name: Constantine
clues: At my death in 337 I was honoured both as a Christian and as a deified emperor.
I paid for churches, including St Peter's Basilica.
I called the bishops together at Nicaea to settle Christian doctrine.
I converted to Christianity, and in 313 the Edict of Milan proclaimed toleration.

people.name: Theodosius
clues: In 391 I ended state support for all cults but one.
I emptied the temple of the hearth goddess.
I put out the sacred fire the Vestals had tended for centuries.
In 380 I made Christianity the official religion of the empire.

places.name: Troy
places.why: The city in Asia Minor destroyed by the Greeks, from which Aeneas fled with sacred objects, according to legend.

places.name: Naples
places.why: Sailors here hailed Augustus shortly before his death in AD 14 as the source of their lives and safe voyages.

places.name: Carthage
places.why: The North African power whose wars with Rome saw the sacred chickens thrown overboard in 249 BC and the Great Mother brought in during 206 BC.

places.name: Nicaea
places.why: The town in Asia Minor where Constantine gathered the bishops to settle Christian doctrine.

places.name: Milan
places.why: The Edict of Milan of 313 proclaimed toleration for Christians.
